drafts.title: Maintain and improve perceived ride comfort on broken pavement and reduce distracting wind noise at highway speeds
drafts.description: Customers experience a smooth, non‑harsh ride on broken or uneven pavement and no distracting wind noise at highway speeds so long-distance and highway driving feels comfortable and non-fatiguing.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: 1) On a standardized rough‑road route (predefined broken‑pavement loop) driven at 30–50 mph, >=80% of a 20‑person representative customer panel rate ride comfort >=4/5. 2) At steady speeds above 70 mph on a straight test section, A‑weighted cabin noise measured at the driver's ear is <=68 dB(A).
assumptions: Test panels use representative US customer demographic (age, height) and repeatable route; weather conditions are within normal range (no heavy rain).
Measurement protocol and cabin microphone position follow an internal NVH test standard; current baseline vehicle is available for benchmarking if needed.
uncertainties: Trade‑offs between ride comfort improvements and sporty handling (customer preference variations).
Exterior noise can vary with optional roof/trim packages and wheel size; results assume production‑standard configurations.

drafts.title: Make lane‑keeping assist feel smooth and predictable in curves (avoid abrupt steering corrections)
drafts.description: When lane‑keeping assist is engaged on highways and curved roads customers feel the system steers smoothly and predictably without sudden or nervous corrections.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a standardized highway curved‑road test at 65–75 mph with 20 representative drivers, >=90% of participants rate the lane‑keeping behaviour as 'smooth/predictable' (>=4/5) and the system completes the test route without an abrupt correction event as judged by the test drivers in >=95% of runs.
assumptions: Tests run on well‑marked highways with lane lines visible and dry conditions; driver attention and readiness requirements remain as today.
Customer panel reflects typical US drivers and includes both users who have used lane assist before and those who have not.
uncertainties: Edge cases (poor lane markings, heavy crosswind, construction zones) may still require conservative behaviour to ensure safety, which can feel intrusive.
Perception of 'smooth' is subjective and may vary by driver preference for more/less intervention.

drafts.title: Plan long trips and find compatible fast chargers so a 600‑mile journey is practical and not confusing
drafts.description: When customers plan long trips, the vehicle presents a clear route with compatible fast‑charging stops and minimizes confusion by showing charger compatibility, estimated stop durations and total on‑route charging time so a 600‑mile trip is practical to execute.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: On a set of representative 600‑mile mixed‑condition routes, the vehicle's trip planner identifies at least one compatible high‑power charging stop (correct connector/network) for each required charge and presents a route with no more than two charging stops and a cumulative estimated on‑route charging time <=40 minutes in >=90% of tested routes. The planner finds a compatible charger within 5 minutes in >=95% of route planning operations.
assumptions: The vehicle has live access to charging network availability/status and connector mappings (agreements with charging networks or standardized roaming data).
Target routes use commonly available fast chargers and typical US interstate infrastructure; charger power capabilities and actual charging speeds follow publicly available network data.
uncertainties: Real‑world charger availability and queuing at third‑party stations can vary and may increase actual stop time.
Different driver charging preferences (state-of-charge at stop, maximum acceptable stop duration) may require personalization.

drafts.title: Make the charge‑port light show charging state at a glance from outside the car
drafts.description: Customers can quickly tell if the vehicle is not charging, charging, or fully charged by a clear, easily visible indicator at the charge port without needing to approach the vehicle or open an app.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: The exterior charge‑port indicator conveys three visually distinct states (not charging / charging / fully charged) readable from 2 meters in daylight. In a blind test with 20 observers, the correct charging state is identified >=95% of the time.
assumptions: Observers have normal vision and tests are conducted in typical daylight conditions; indicator brightness meets applicable vehicle exterior lighting constraints.
Indicator design uses distinct colors and/or blinking patterns to represent states.
uncertainties: Visibility may vary with aftermarket covers, dirt, or snow; durability of exterior indicator over time is unknown.
Color perception differences (e.g., colorblind users) should be considered in final design.
